Intentional
in-TEN-shun-ul
adjective
From Latin intentio, a stretching toward, purpose, aim. A plain and useful English word meaning done on purpose, deliberate. In the evangelical subculture of the 2000s-2010s it swelled into a near-sacred buzzword — 'intentional discipleship,' 'intentional community,' 'living intentionally' — doing much branding and little real work.

Biblical Verdict

🟠
Examine
A fine kernel (purposeful living) inflated into a buzzword that brands ordinary planning as spirituality; recover the virtue, drop the halo, weigh the doing.

Biblical Definition

The kernel is biblical and good: Scripture commends purposeful, deliberate living over drift and sloth. 'See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil' (Eph. 5:15-16); 'Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee. Ponder the path of thy feet' (Prov. 4:25-26). The wise man 'looketh well to his going' (Prov. 14:15); the builder first 'sitteth not down... and counteth the cost' (Luke 14:28); Daniel 'purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself' (Dan. 1:8). To be deliberate — to plan, to aim, to choose the good on purpose rather than by accident — is simple Christian wisdom. So far the word names a real virtue. The trouble is not the kernel but the inflation: a humble adjective for 'on purpose' has been crowned as if deliberateness were itself a high spiritual attainment.

Webster 1828 Definition

A plain word for 'on purpose,' with a fine biblical kernel (Eph. 5:15-16), inflated into an evangelical buzzword that dresses ordinary planning as spiritual achievement — doing more branding than work.

INTENTIONAL, adjective. Done on purpose; deliberate; aimed.

From Latin intentio, a stretching toward, purpose — a plain and useful word.

Sound kernel: purposeful living over drift — 'redeeming the time' (Eph. 5:16); 'ponder the path of thy feet' (Prov. 4:26).

Corrupt drift: an evangelical buzzword ('intentional community,' 'living intentionally') that dresses ordinary planning as spiritual achievement — branding in place of substance.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 5:15-16 — "See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil."

Proverbs 4:26 — "Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established."

Luke 14:28 — "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?"

Daniel 1:8 — "But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself."

James 1:22 — "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."

Modern Corruption

A plain adjective for 'deliberate' is inflated into a near-sacred buzzword, so that calling a thing 'intentional' makes ordinary planning feel spiritual — a word doing more branding than work.

expand to see more

The corruption is inflation, not falsehood. 'Intentional' simply means 'on purpose,' and being purposeful is a genuine biblical virtue — 'redeeming the time' (Eph. 5:16), pondering the path (Prov. 4:26), counting the cost (Luke 14:28). The trouble began when the evangelical subculture promoted the adjective to a spiritual rank, so that prefixing 'intentional' to any ordinary activity — intentional coffee, intentional friendship, intentional parenting — lent it an air of holy seriousness it had not earned. The word became a halo: to call a thing 'intentional' was to signal depth and devotion, while often describing nothing more than what 'on purpose' already says. It is branding vocabulary, and like all such vocabulary it can substitute the label for the labor.

The subtler danger is that intending feels like doing. 'I'm being really intentional about this' can become a way of crediting oneself for a resolve never carried out — the deliberateness admired, the deed undone. But Scripture weighs the doing, not the intending: 'be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves' (James 1:22); 'not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord... but he that doeth the will of my Father' (Matt. 7:21). Daniel's purposing in his heart (Dan. 1:8) was honored because it issued in a refusal he actually made and a cost he actually paid. A purpose that warms the conscience but never moves the hands is the very self-deception James warns against, dressed in a fashionable word.

The recovery is to keep the kernel and drop the inflation. Be deliberate — genuinely; plan, aim, choose the good on purpose, redeem the time in evil days (Eph. 5:16). But do not mistake the adjective for an attainment, and do not let 'intentional' become a badge worn in place of obedience done. The mark of a purposeful Christian is not that he describes his life as 'intentional' but that his ways are 'established' (Prov. 4:26) in actual, costly, completed obedience. Let the word mean what it has always plainly meant, and let the deeds, not the branding, bear the weight.

Hebrew Roots

From Latin intentio, purpose; a plain word for 'deliberate' with a fine kernel (Eph. 5:15-16), inflated into a buzzword. Recover purposeful living, drop the halo, and weigh the doing over the intending (James 1:22).

expand to see more

Latin: intentio, a stretching toward, purpose, aim — the plain root of 'on purpose.'

Sound kernel: Eph. 5:15-16 and Prov. 4:26 — circumspect, deliberate walking; redeeming the time.

The test: James 1:22, 'doers of the word, and not hearers only' — the deed, not the intention, bears the weight.

Usage

"He was 'being intentional' about discipleship for a year and discipled no one; Scripture weighs the doing, not the intending."

"A plain word for 'on purpose' got a halo, and prefixing 'intentional' began to lend ordinary errands an unearned air of devotion."

"Be deliberate in earnest — count the cost, ponder the path — but let the deeds, not the branding, bear the weight."
